notes.title: Devlog #5
notes.content:
Hello, this is Team Samoyed! Teamfight Manager 2 will be consistently sharing its development process through development logs every 2–3 weeks. We truly appreciate your interest.

In this edition, we will be discussing recruitment, training, and balance patches.

[h2]Development Direction[/h2]

Before diving into the details, we'd like to first talk about the current development status and direction of Teamfight Manager 2. Teamfight Manager 2 features quite complex and diverse simulation elements, and fine-tuning these components to create depth is a truly challenging task.

Therefore, even if it means lacking some depth and content scale initially, our plan for Teamfight Manager 2 is to first complete the overall system and then refine the game together with our users through the Early Access process, enhancing its completeness.

To achieve this, Teamfight Manager 2 development is planned to proceed through the following major steps:

[olist]
[*] Implement match simulation to a playable level (Completed)
[*] Implement foundational team management systems outside of matches, such as recruitment, training, financial management, staff, etc. (In Progress)
[*] Improve and experiment with match simulation, rules, etc., implement champions (Planned)
[*] Implement and stabilize game features like tutorials, multiplayer, Workshop support, etc. (Planned)
[*] Diversify overall game content, including team management, and add more depth (Planned)
[*] Start Early Access once the minimum game depth and content volume for EA are ready
[/olist]

We are currently in the phase of sequentially implementing the foundational systems, corresponding to step 2 in the overall process goals. Since this is the stage of creating the overall flow of how features work before filling in internal content, you might notice a lack of overall depth and quality, or gaps in various parts of the system. Content refinement work to add depth to the game is planned after the overall game framework is established, so please keep this development flow in mind when reading the dev logs.

[h2]Recruitment[/h2]

The player recruitment and transfer system in Teamfight Manager 2 is being implemented to follow a more realistic contract process. However, given the game's nature—set in a fictional sports league rather than a real-world sport—we are aiming for a system that is intuitive and easy to understand, yet offers sufficiently diverse choices, rather than directly replicating complex real-world contract methods.

The recruitment process has been implemented as follows: Negotiate the transfer fee with the team -> Discuss detailed contract terms with the player after the transfer negotiation is complete -> Finalize the player signing once contract conditions are agreed upon.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/a218931f010f7487914db9bc3509ff9d3816c643.png[/img]

This is the player transfer fee negotiation screen. While we are considering adding various options related to the transfer fee later, only the function to negotiate the fee amount is currently implemented. The Head Coach Analysis in the top right will also be added after the coaching staff-related features are implemented.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/4cb5102509adb8f2025e9a5c35ff174f567d8144.png[/img]

During the transfer fee negotiation process, negotiations might break down entirely if the opposing team doesn't want to sell the player, or if the proposed terms are unreasonable. Alternatively, the opposing team might counter-propose different conditions.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/ef9427352b1b59b625aecc3b7ff5d7ba1c527e52.png[/img]

Once negotiations regarding the transfer fee are completed, you can discuss direct contract conditions with the player.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/712e9981784a18f32119efa5ff35838fb63d183c.png[/img]

Currently, only conditions regarding salary and contract duration can be negotiated and offered, but the feature to add various option clauses on the right is also planned.

There is a lot of room for improvement in the transfer simulation aspect. We believe the process of recruiting players becomes more interesting as diverse scenarios emerge based on various factors, such as differences in the transfer process depending on the relationship between the player and the team, emotions running high during negotiations, teams' operational plans for the season, players' goals, etc. For now, only the most basic transfer and recruitment logic and conditions are implemented. Many improvements to the transfer and recruitment process are planned after implementing various foundational systems like coaching staff and scouting.

[h2]Training[/h2]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/b51bc336403f318081f73a9a1593e20c74168e28.png[/img]

For training, you can set the team's basic training plan through 10 program settings. The team training plan is a common training schedule that all teams will use by default. If you want to assign different training for specific players, it is also possible to adjust their training individually.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/70ec7b7fc0037aa833adda0c88226dc49ae76e37.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/e25d0ad4af3b45dcdd6b530800a37c4c7ff6f519.png[/img]

In the individual training plan, you can change some training programs based on the common program like this.

Currently, training is implemented only as a structure where player stats grow appropriately based on the assigned program and the player's potential value. Training is also scheduled for content improvements after various other systems are implemented.

[h2]Balance Patch[/h2]

The balance patch system in Teamfight Manager 2 is broadly divided into three stages:

[list]
[*] Minor Patch: Patches occurring at short intervals during the regular season. Only low-intensity balance adjustments affecting a small number of champions are made.
[*] Major Patch: Patches occurring about 3-4 times a year, implementing higher-intensity balance patches and simultaneously adding one new champion.
[*] Season Patch: A patch occurring once a year, featuring the largest-scale balance patch along with the addition of new champions. Season patches include not only champion balance adjustments but also changes to overall game rules, such as tower damage, attack speed, jungle monster experience amounts, etc.
[/list]

In this way, we aim to provide patch notes that feel closer to how actual game patches occur. Additionally, through season patches, we intend to allow fundamental game rules to change annually, continuously providing a slightly fresh feel.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/ac9095302e478aceac6e325a0034772ad9c3a1bb.png[/img]

At the same time, as shown in the image, we have widened the scope of changes resulting from patches by allowing adjustments to many more elements than in the previous game. In Teamfight Manager 2, balance patches can affect almost all numerical values that determine a skill's basic operation, such as basic range, area of effect, how each skill scales with stats (coefficients), action duration (cast time), etc.

[h3]Patch Algorithm[/h3]

Determining which target and which element the automatic patch will adjust is also a very important factor. If already strong champions are continuously buffed, or already weak champions are continuously nerfed, it's difficult to bring meaningful changes to gameplay, no matter how many different elements are changed.

The goal of the patch algorithm in Teamfight Manager 2 is fundamentally to continuously bring about changes in the utilized champion pool. We aim to prevent situations where certain champions maintain high pick rates for several seasons, or where specific champions are consistently almost never selected. As the patch algorithm is something that needs continuous observation, we will cover the detailed content in a future development log.

That concludes this development log! Thank you for reading this lengthy post. We look forward to seeing you in the next update!

notes.title: Devlog #4
notes.content:
Hello, this is Team Samoyed! Teamfight Manager 2 will be consistently sharing its development process through development logs every 2–3 weeks. We truly appreciate your interest.

In this edition, we will be discussing the locker room content.

[h2]Locker Room Feedback[/h2]

In the previous game, the locker room feedback feature eventually became nothing more than a tedious, repetitive task as the game progressed. With Teamfight Manager 2, we want the locker room feedback to remain engaging and meaningful throughout.

To achieve this, the overall direction we intend for the locker room feedback in Teamfight Manager 2 is as follows:

[list]
[*] Each option available in the locker room will carry sufficient meaning, yet not have an overwhelming impact.
[*] The outcome of each option will not feel excessively random.
[/list]

Based on this direction, here is what the current locker room content under development looks like:

[img]https://images.steamusercontent.com/ugc/37824255576552198/C1B8269F65F5E8D174F781B3D2C2CB094562E4E9/?imw=1024&imh=576&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=true[/img]

After a match, in the locker room the coach can choose either not to provide any feedback or to listen to what each player has to say. Depending on the choice made, players’ confidence and dissatisfaction stats will change.

Furthermore, as shown in the image, if the coach chooses to listen to a player’s feedback request, they can directly view and verify the scene that the player wants to comment on.

[img]https://images.steamusercontent.com/ugc/37824255576553195/BF5D530E2B35C631C1F854C480A9EBDB069EF21B/?imw=5000&imh=5000&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=false[/img]

After confirming the scene where a player is visibly dissatisfied, you can choose an option to give feedback. In the scene shown, player dalonge opted to retreat early, judging the situation to be dangerous while pushing the top lane alongside player Biubiu, who, by persisting in the fight, ultimately died. What would be the appropriate choice in this situation?

[img]https://images.steamusercontent.com/ugc/37824255576554023/12BC7C998B31A549B7FEBB49ED0011E63890D735/?imw=1024&imh=576&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=true[/img]

This image shows a scenario where Biubiu is deemed to have made the wrong decision, with the coach pointing out Biubiu’s mistake. As a result, dalonge’s confidence increases while Biubiu’s dissatisfaction grows. You can choose to give feedback honestly according to what you believe is right, or consider the players’ confidence and dissatisfaction to adjust your feedback appropriately. Ultimately, the coach must make the choice that best positions the team for success.

[h2]Confidence, Dissatisfaction[/h2]

Now, let’s explore the roles of the confidence and dissatisfaction stats that are affected by the locker room content.

[list]
[*] Confidence: Influences a player’s proactive play. Players with low confidence tend to avoid aggressive roaming and combat, opting instead for a more passive approach.
[*] Dissatisfaction: Players with high dissatisfaction tend to ignore the coach’s instructions. They are less likely to follow assigned tactics and may play in an overly independent manner. Accumulated dissatisfaction can reduce training efficiency and might even prompt a player to request a transfer. [/list]

These two stats differ from the base stats (such as mechanics, decision-making, mental strength, focus, etc.) in that they are influenced solely by team management content like the locker room. Although their overall impact is relatively minor compared to base stats, managing your team so that overall confidence remains high and dissatisfaction is kept low can lead to performance that exceeds what base stats alone would predict.

Thus, the current locker room content is being designed as a long-term management system that coordinates each player over multiple matches, based on the two stats: confidence and dissatisfaction.

[h2]Traits[/h2]

Additionally, in Teamfight Manager 2 we plan to shift the role of traits from directly affecting in-game play (as in the previous game) to influencing team management. With a broader range of stats and changes in how these stats function compared to the previous game, traits can no longer operate in the same way. Instead, we are clearly shifting their role toward team management, adding depth to the coach’s considerations when assembling a squad. Below are a few examples of the traits we are planning under this new direction:

[list]
[*] "Big-game choker": In a best-of-five series, reduces confidence by 5.
[*] "Show-off": Doubles the chance of requesting feedback.
[*] "Avoidant": If the coach does not provide feedback, increases confidence by 2; if feedback is given, decreases confidence by 2.
[*] "Meddlesome": Improves the relationship between players who do not get along by 1% each week.
[*] "Sensitive": Causes confidence and dissatisfaction to fluctuate twice as much.
[*] "Extrovert": During tactical training, increases team relationship stats with extroverted players by an additional 10% and boosts the chance of requesting feedback by 30%.
[/list]

As illustrated in these examples, player traits operate as factors that influence team management based on confidence, dissatisfaction, and team relationship stats. Even if overall team stats are somewhat low, assembling players with suitable traits can simplify team management and, by maintaining high team relationships and confidence with low dissatisfaction, may lead to performance beyond the base stats.

In this way, Teamfight Manager 2 is continuously exploring how to allow coaches to build and manage their squads according to their objectives, maximizing performance within the constraints of their budgets through a system based on traits, confidence, dissatisfaction, and team relationship stats.

[h2]Observing[/h2]

Additionally, while developing the locker room feedback content, we also tackled the implementation of an in-game observing feature. Originally, the intent was to display the entire game layout on one screen; however, by skipping intermediate steps and jumping directly to specific scenes, it became difficult to tell from the full-screen view exactly which situation the current feedback was based on. Moreover, as we continuously refine the in-game player AI, simultaneous events occurring in different parts of the map have made it even harder to follow the overall game flow on a single screen.

To resolve these issues, we implemented an observing function that shows a magnified view of the area where a specific event is taking place. Based on this, we also developed a “Highlights Only” feature in matches.

[img]https://images.steamusercontent.com/ugc/37824255576554327/39DF52C20D9CC16E18E189D5D850B8328A2FDC3C/?imw=5000&imh=5000&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=false[/img]

In “Highlights Only” mode, as shown in the image above, the game plays at a fast pace and when a highlight moment occurs, that scene is enlarged and played.

That concludes this development log! Thank you for reading this lengthy post. We look forward to seeing you in the next update!

notes.title: Devlog #3
notes.content:
Hello, this is Team Samoyed!

Teamfight Manager 2 will be sharing consistent development logs every 2–3 weeks to keep you updated on our progress. We appreciate your interest and suppor

In this edition, we’re covering the match schedule configuration and the ban/pick AI.

[h2]Match Schedule Configuration[/h2]

In the previous game, a season was played as a league over one year, followed by a World Championship once the league ended. Moreover, there wasn’t a notion of specific dates—the game’s time advanced in one-week increments. That format was chosen because the previous game was designed for a lighter playstyle, aiming for fast-paced matches that emphasized the ban/pick process.

However, Teamfight Manager 2 is targeting a more realistic and complex management experience. In-game elements such as ban/pick and tactics have become significantly more intricate and weighty compared to the previous title. Accordingly, we have revised the match scheduling process as follows:

[list]
[*] Each schedule is now organized on a daily basis.
[*] Matches are no longer grouped in one-week bundles. Instead, on each day, a set number of matches are played per tournament.
[/list]

In addition, the overall tournament structure for a season has been changed as follows: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/d43c200430532b0e327f3c9732c6992f4ce5cc91.png[/img] 

[i]Icons representing each league’s teams[/i]

[list]
[*] There are four leagues—Korea, China, Europe, and North America—each consisting of 10 teams.
[*] Each league conducts two seasons per year: a Spring Season and a Summer Season.
[*] Each league is divided into a regular season and playoffs, with the top 6 teams from the regular season advancing to the playoffs.
[*] Playoffs follow a double-elimination format.
[*] International competitions consist of two tournaments: the Masters Cup and the Champions Cup. The top teams from the Spring Season qualify for the Masters Cup, and the top teams from the Summer Season qualify for the Champions Cup. Seeding for each league in international play may vary each year based on performance.
[*] For teams that do not qualify for the Masters or Champions Cup, a separate tournament is held between rival leagues (Korea–China and Europe–North America).
[*] Player recruitment is permitted from the end of the Champions Cup until the start of the Spring Season, and from the end of the Masters Cup until the start of the Summer Season.
[/list]

For international competitions, the current plan is for 16 teams to qualify, divided into groups of 4 for a group stage, followed by a single-elimination tournament among the top 8 teams. However, after further testing, this format may be altered. We are also considering adding other regional leagues or a secondary division, and we’re still deliberating on finer details such as whether each regional league should have its own slightly different format. These elements may change as development progresses.

With Teamfight Manager 2, as matches have become much more complex, there are significantly more factors to research and prepare compared to the previous game. The new schedule is intended to give you more time between matches to analyze other teams’ data, manage your team’s finances, prepare training and tactics, and scout new players. We’ll introduce these various management elements one by one in future development logs.

[h2]Ban/Pick AI[/h2]

As the match simulation has evolved, significant changes were also needed for the ban/pick AI used by opposing teams. The biggest difference from the previous game is the introduction of positions—now, when selecting champions, you must also decide which position to assign each one.

For smooth testing, we initially continued using the existing ban/pick AI. However, we discovered that the old AI tended to use a single champion in too many different positions. Because it tested multiple combinations and inferred a champion’s value based on team compositions, the previous AI would often deploy a seemingly strong champion into any available position. While a moderate degree of versatility can be interesting, having every champion play every position quickly becomes confusing and unrealistic. Therefore, we needed to adjust the system so that each champion is primarily used in the position where they perform most efficiently. Of course, this issue is complex—it’s tied not only to the ban/pick AI but also to champion balance and game rules—so we are continuously experimenting with various approaches.

In addition, Teamfight Manager 2 sets several new objectives for the ban/pick phase, and we are working to adapt the system accordingly:

[list]
[*] Reflecting Team Identity: We want each team’s ban/pick style to vary slightly based on the coach’s preferences. Some teams might focus exclusively on a “Plan A,” while others might react flexibly based on the draft, opting to ban the opponent’s key picks or to execute effective counters.
[*] League-Specific Tendencies: Building on each team’s identity and the inherent traits of players in each league, our goal is to enable each league to develop its own key picks and meta. This way, in international competitions, teams will encounter a new style of play compared to their domestic league—and overcoming that challenge will be essential for success.
[*] Preventing Repetitive Strategies: We’re also refining the AI so that if a player discovers a successful ban/pick or tactic, the AI can better counter its repeated use. The aim is to encourage players to continuously innovate and improve their strategies, rather than sticking to the same approach.
[/list]

Although these goals are challenging and it’s uncertain how fully they can be achieved, we are committed to doing our best to realize this vision.

To quickly review the changes in the ban/pick AI—as mentioned in previous logs—we have implemented a simulator. In this simulator, various ban/pick AIs can be deployed to each team, and matches are automatically simulated between teams. You can then review each team’s win rate, the champions they selected, and the complete lists of bans and picks from each match. Using these statistical data, we compare the win rates of the old ban/pick AI with the newly implemented one, as well as examine champion usage by position, all to drive further improvements in our ban/pick system.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/87f63e63420fdbd19a3513ea7924e7a805c0e3e6.png[/img]

The image above shows data from the simulator indicating which champions were chosen for the first two bans by each ban/pick AI. The image on the left represents the bans chosen by the original AI, while the one on the right shows the bans selected by the improved AI. Previously, because the AI relied solely on probabilistic exploration, the bans varied too much from match to match and often failed to effectively counter the opponent’s strongest picks. We have now adjusted it so that the AI prioritizes banning the most threatening champions during the ban phase in line with its tactical approach.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/8291a66b36000c45b212b4c89730003ec3fe0ff7.png[/img]

Additionally, the image above displays a list of the top five champions most frequently used in the top lane by four different teams in our simulation. Comparing these lists shows that while certain strong champions are commonly selected for that lane, there are subtle variations in picks that reflect each team’s unique identity and tactics. This ensures that while teams avoid choosing champions that feel out of place, they can still maintain a distinct team flavor in their ban/pick strategy.

[h2]Simulation Improvements[/h2]

Alongside these efforts, we are continuously working to improve the in-game simulation AI. Currently, the average match lasts around 6 minutes, with most matches falling within a 4- to 8-minute range. Although the optimal match duration may change based on further playtesting, our goal is to strike a balance—ensuring matches are not so long as to become tedious, while also avoiding a pace that feels overwhelmingly frantic as match phases pass too quickly. At present, we’re aiming for the laning phase to conclude in roughly 3 minutes, followed by another 3 minutes for the mid-to-late game phase, which we believe creates a good overall flow.

Of course, with longer match times, we are also considering the addition of features that allow players to fast-forward through certain parts of a match—such as 2x or 3x speed options or the ability to view only key moments.

That’s it for this development log! Thank you for taking the time to read this lengthy post. We look forward to seeing you in the next update!

notes.title: Devlog #2
notes.content:
Hello, this is Team Samoyed!

Teamfight Manager 2 will be sharing consistent development logs every 2–3 weeks to keep you updated on our progress. We appreciate your interest and support.

In this edition, we’ll take a closer look at how player stats, tactics, and related elements function within the match engine.

[h2]Player Stats[/h2]

In Teamfight Manager 2, the primary goal for player stats is to ensure that each stat holds its own unique value. In the previous game, while stats such as Attack, Defense, and Champion Mastery each played a different role, it was hard to say that each stat truly had a distinct value. This was also tied to the game’s management elements—in the previous title, you started in an amateur league, and as time went on, the overall team stats would gradually increase until, by winning the World Championship, you’d see the game’s ending. In such a system, as stats and finances steadily grow, there’s little reason to specifically recruit a player with one particular stat; you’d simply use the player with the higher overall stats.

However, when your budget is limited and you must construct your squad carefully, the decision becomes more nuanced. For instance, if you have two players both with a total stat sum of 50—one with 40 Attack and 10 Defense versus another with 10 Attack and 40 Defense—you need to deliberate which balance of attributes better fits your strategy. With limited funds, every point matters, and choosing the best possible player within your budget becomes essential.

As we will elaborate in future logs, Teamfight Manager 2 is designed with a more realistic approach to team management. We wanted to ensure that when you manage your squad, you’ll face deep strategic decisions about how to compose your team.

Before diving into those aspects further, let’s review the basic components that make up a player’s stats:

[list]
[*] Mechanics: Influences the player’s control abilities. Higher mechanics mean you’re better at landing non-targeted skills and evading enemy attacks. (This was briefly mentioned in previous logs.)
[*] Decision-making: Affects the player’s judgment. A player with high decision-making can better predict enemy gank risks, determine the proper timing for exchanges, and more accurately assess the pros and cons of various tactical maneuvers.
[*] Mental Strength: Impacts a player’s mental resilience. Players with low mental strength might perform poorly in lane (e.g., suffering consecutive solo kills) or see their stats sharply drop under high-pressure conditions.
[*] Focus: Plays a key role in the late game. Players with low focus are more prone to mistakes as the game prolongs, resulting in an overall drop in performance.
[*] Champion Proficiency: When a player chooses their preferred champion, their overall performance significantly increases; conversely, playing a non-preferred champion causes a marked drop.
[*] Position Proficiency: Playing in a role in which you lack proficiency leads to a reduction in overall performance
 [/list]

In this development log, we introduce a more complex interplay of scenarios. To help illustrate, let’s first examine the champion compositions for both teams featured in this log.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/01d1dddb9c78da0d1e2d27324373c402c7e6d0e8.png[/img]

For the Blue Team, from the top lane onward, the composition is Swordsman, Ninja, Archer, and Fighter; for the Red Team, it is Dual Blader, Lancer, Sniper, and Executioner.

[img]https://images.steamusercontent.com/ugc/37821548562956766/9566AD45D2FA4B8A9A2DEE6D1CCC3ADDA4226943/?imw=5000&imh=5000&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=false[/img]

In the composition above, notice an early-match scene where the Fighter successfully makes a top lane intervention. Although the sequence is somewhat lengthy and complex, let’s break it down step by step:

[olist]
[*] The Fighter is the Blue Team’s Support, and the Archer is the Bottom laner. At this moment, the bottom lane is heavily pushed, and the opposing Support, Executioner, is visible in the lane.
[*] A fight has broken out in the top jungle, and with the support joining the skirmish, a favorable situation could be created.
[*] The Fighter moves to the top lane and successfully takes down the enemy top laner.
[/olist]

A player with high decision-making can, as illustrated above, assess diverse in-game situations accurately—allowing them to act ahead of the enemy or anticipate their moves.

As seen here, while Mechanics and Decision-making both directly impact a player’s in-game AI, they influence different aspects: Mechanics govern the fine details of control, whereas Decision-making governs the evaluation of situations and the selection of appropriate actions.

Additionally, Mental Strength, Focus, Champion Proficiency, and Position Proficiency act as indirect modifiers that adjust the core in-game performance represented by Mechanics and Decision-making under various circumstances.

Now, let’s revisit team management from a broader perspective. When constructing your squad on a limited budget, you must align your roster with the meta and your strategic vision. For example, you might adopt one of the following strategies:

[list]
[*] Aggressive Early Pressure: If your goal is to secure an early or mid-game advantage and finish the game quickly, you might be willing to sacrifice some Mental Strength or Focus. The idea is to gain an early edge—since failing to do so often results in defeat later. In this case, building your squad around high Mechanics and Decision-making (even if Mental Strength and Focus are slightly lower) can create effective synergy for early picks and rapid execution.
[*] Late-game Scaling: Conversely, if you plan to endure the early game and aim for a late-game victory, you’ll favor players with high Focus. Additionally, if your draft strategy revolves around coordinated, target-focused engagements, players with lower Mechanics might suffice as long as their Decision-making is strong.
[*] Top Lane Emphasis: Alternatively, if the top lane is pivotal to your strategy, you might choose a player with exceptionally high stats for that position, while filling the other lanes with players whose stats are comparatively lower but still adequate for supporting roles—allowing you to push the top lane effectively.
[/list]

This approach—assigning each stat a unique role, building your squad accordingly, and integrating these choices with your tactics and champion picks—is the core design philosophy of Teamfight Manager 2. Note that the stat system is not yet finalized; as development progresses, if we discover an even better configuration that aligns with our goals, further adjustments may be made.

Furthermore, additional attributes such as Confidence, Complaints, Team Relationships, and Communication Levels are still in the works, and we will cover those in future development logs!

[h2]Tactics[/h2]

While the tactics system isn’t completely finalized, we’ll briefly discuss the tactics currently implemented and how they operate.

[h3]Team Tactics[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/099dcd52428c75c32fedda85c2a06a941171f7cd.png[/img]

Team tactics affect the overall play direction of the entire team.

[list]
[*] Main Target Lane: Determines whether the team should attack the top or bottom tower first. When the initiative is secured, players focus on breaking the designated lane’s tower.
[*] Offensive Tactics: After one tower falls, decide whether to pressure the already pushed lane or concentrate on breaking the intact tower.
[*] Defensive Tactics: With a passive approach, only the minimal number of players defend the tower while the rest continue pressuring their lanes. With an aggressive approach, more players commit to keeping the tower intact.
[*] Combat Style: An aggressive stance means players will group together to initiate fights or force engagements, whereas a passive stance means they stick together, avoiding uncertain skirmishes and only engaging when a clear advantage is present.
[/list]

[img]https://images.steamusercontent.com/ugc/37821548562957020/86264B67A2C3DD6588A5C882BC19C38E63F8E1E1/?imw=5000&imh=5000&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=false[/img]

The image above shows a play shaped by team tactics. Through a bottom lane gank, the team manages to take out the enemy Support, Executioner, and the Blue Team then focuses their main target on the bottom lane. Consequently, they pressure the bottom lane while even the top laner, the Swordsman, joins the assault.

Conversely, the Red Team adopts an aggressive defensive tactic. In that scenario, the Lancer roams the jungle and defends the bottom lane as the situation grows perilous. Had the defensive tactic been passive and the Jungler prioritized personal growth, the focus might have shifted from tower defense to safe farming.

[h3]Individual Tactics[/h3]

[h4]Laner[/h4]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/7a900c8bc3b65d3ed3af6811eb8f0fe4dc5fa876.png[/img]
[h4]Jungler[/h4]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45467379/ee8d21f366a9bd03d6a06f68303b454aa841400e.png[/img]

There are slight differences between laners and junglers regarding individual tactics. Let’s start with the shared element—play style:

[list]
[*] Play Style: A self-focused player focuses primarily on their own growth, rarely leaving their lane even if nearby fights occur or support is requested—unless absolutely necessary. In contrast, a support-focused player prioritizes assisting teammates, even if it means sacrificing some personal growth.
[/list]

For laners, the tactical considerations include:

[list]
[*] Combat Style: An aggressive laner actively engages in early trades and seeks out kills, while passive laner focuses on conserving health and growing safely.
[*] Initiative Utilization: When choosing to pressure, a laner with the initiative will push their lane harder, and under other conditions may be more inclined to roam to other lanes. (For example, as noted earlier, if the initiative utilization focuses on lane pressure, the Fighter's roaming is less likely to occur.)
[/list]

For junglers, the tactical design includes:

[list]
[*] Path Planning: Balances the focus between jungle farming and gank participation.
[*] Intervention Style: Determines how the jungler targets opponents during engagements. If set to counter-jungle, the jungler will harass the enemy jungle and steal camps; otherwise, they prioritize ganks based on specific conditions in designated lanes.
[/list]

The current tactical implementations operate as described above, though since the overall game framework is still being finalized, further playtesting is needed. For example, we are considering enhancements such as:

[list]
[*] Instead of selecting from a set of options, using a slider to adjust the intensity of a tactic might be more suitable.
[*] As the game progresses from early to mid to late stages, more granular tactical adjustments may be necessary.
[*] Adding additional tactical options, such as tower dive attempts.
[/list]

[h3]Calls[/h3]

Lastly, let’s briefly discuss the concept of “calls,” which is still under development.

[img]https://images.steamusercontent.com/ugc/37821548562957117/DCB861DEEFF67F35E6B10C6551B43A53BBF9C0F0/?imw=5000&imh=5000&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=false[/img]

Within the match engine simulation, players make “calls” during engagements, retreats, and other situations. Calls are a way to share information about the game state and personal decisions—for example, calling to group for a fight, to retreat, or to indicate that an enemy has disappeared. In the image above, you can see that while most teammates issue calls, the Sniper retreats during the early team fight. Fortunately, the team still secures the win, but differences in calls and team synergy can ultimately affect the outcome.

We are working on adding a variety of call types and developing a system to visually display them so that players can assess team coordination and information sharing.

[h2]Technical Insights[/h2]

In this section, we’ll briefly explain how we are technically implementing the design directions mentioned above.

[h3]Stat Balancing[/h3]

If stat balance is lost, certain attributes may become entirely useless. Our balancing goals for player stats are as follows:

[list]
[*] On average, each point in any stat should have similar value.
[*] The effectiveness of each stat may vary slightly depending on the champion—some champions might benefit more from Mechanics, while others gain more from Focus.
[*] Tactics can also influence the relative value of each stat.
[/list]

These differences mean that even teams with similar overall strength can perform very differently based on how they are managed. In drafting and tactical planning, the aim is to maximize each player’s strengths, pushing the limits of their capabilities.

The challenge is to verify and adjust whether these balancing goals are being met. Relying solely on playtesting is insufficient, so we use statistical data to verify that outcomes align with our goals.

To this end, we’ve built a tool that runs countless simulations across various stat configurations and game scenarios, generating data for balancing purposes. Running 1,000 match simulations takes at most five minutes, providing us with a broad range of research data and statistical insights.
Of course, the simulation data might not perfectly mirror actual gameplay (since bans, picks, and other factors can cause significant variations), but our primary focus is ensuring that every element feels meaningful and engaging to the player. We continually combine playtesting with statistical analysis to refine the match engine.

[h3]Evaluating Tactical Impact[/h3]

For tactics, we are examining their impact from two main perspectives:

[list]
[*] When all other factors (player stats, champion compositions, etc.) are held constant, we measure the win rate differences that result solely from changing tactics.
[*] Across all random matches, we analyze how tactical choices affect in-game metrics. For instance, an aggressive combat style should statistically lead to more kills, and a specific main target lane should correlate with a noticeable difference in the timing of tower destruction.
[/list]

By collecting these statistics, we ensure that the influence of tactics is neither overwhelmingly dominant nor insignificant. In parallel, we conduct test plays to ensure that these tactical differences are tangible and impactful during actual gameplay, continuously refining the match engine as we move forward.

This concludes this development log. Thank you for reading this extensive post, and we look forward to seeing you in the next update!

notes.title: Devlog #1
notes.content:
Hello, this is Team Samoyed!

Teamfight Manager 2 will be sharing consistent development updates every 2–3 weeks through development logs. We appreciate your interest and support!

[h3]Match Engine[/h3]

The first development log will cover the most crucial aspect of the game: the design of the match engine. Since we are still in the early stages of development, many changes are expected. For now, we will briefly outline the direction we are taking with the match engine.

[h3]Game Rules[/h3]

In Teamfight Manager, the team that secures the most kills within one minute wins. This simple rule makes the game easy to understand, but it also has the downside of limiting strategic diversity, which can make the game feel repetitive over time.

With Teamfight Manager 2, we aim to create a deeper game simulation that remains engaging for a longer period. To achieve this, we have moved away from the deathmatch rule and introduced a simplified MOBA-style game structure.
[img]https://steamuserimages-a.akamaihd.net/ugc/37820376621121590/9D58BDBFFC0B397173C2E3119D040FCA52428F21/?imw=2048&imh=1152&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=true[/img]

[list]
[*] Matches are played in a 4v4 format, just like in the previous game.
[*] There are four positions: Top, Jungle, Bottom, and Support.
[*] The map features two lanes, Top and Bottom. The Top position plays in the top lane, while the Bottom and Support positions play in the bottom lane. The Jungle position focuses on farming jungle monsters and ganking.
[*] A leveling system has been introduced. Champions gain experience by killing minions, jungle monsters, destroying towers, and participating in kills. Leveling up increases their stats, and at level 3, they unlock a second skill.
[*] The team that destroys the opponent’s relic first wins.
[/list]

Since this is a fictional game within the game, we are designing the rules to be as simple and intuitive as possible. Our goal is to make it easy for players to understand the game mechanics just by watching a couple of matches.

[h3]Player Actions[/h3]

In Teamfight Manager, player behavior in matches was mostly governed by simple rules, with a few traits influencing AI decisions. However, this often made it feel like the players weren’t actively making decisions.

One of the goals for Teamfight Manager 2’s match engine is to make it feel more like the players are actually controlling the game. For example:
[list]
[*] In Teamfight Manager, players would always attack the closest enemy unless a trait dictated otherwise.
[*] In Teamfight Manager 2, players can choose to target more distant enemies based on their judgment.
[/list]

Additionally, we are reworking how player stats function:
[list]
[*] In Teamfight Manager, player stats (attack, defense, champion proficiency, etc.) directly influenced in-game champion stats. This made it feel like “better players just deal more damage,” which was intuitive but somewhat unrealistic.
[*] In Teamfight Manager 2, player stats no longer directly modify champion stats. Instead, they influence AI decision-making, leading to different playstyles.
   [list]
[*] A player with high mechanics will dodge skill shots more effectively.
[*] A player with high decision-making will make better strategic choices.
[/list]
[/list]

This new system allows for a more dynamic simulation, creating distinct team playstyles, tactics, and in-game situations.

[h3]Champion Design[/h3]

With this shift in direction, champion skills are also being designed to highlight player AI differences.

[img]https://steamuserimages-a.akamaihd.net/ugc/37820376621149304/10352F16B9BF926B47180B43ED8B4447CA7FC084/?imw=1024&imh=320&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=true[/img]
[i]Dual Blader skillfully evades all of Executioner’s attacks, gaining a significant advantage in the battle.[/i]

For example, in the match engine currently in development:
- Dual Blader successfully dodges all of Executioner’s skills, securing an advantage in lane.
- Executioner’s pull skill and Dual Blader’s dash skill have been converted to skill shots.
- Dual Blader’s dash can be used both offensively and defensively, depending on the player’s judgment.

Since these skill shots require precise execution, champions like Dual Blader are more effective when controlled by a player with high mechanics. However, if a player’s mechanics aren’t high enough, the outcome may be drastically different.
[img]https://steamuserimages-a.akamaihd.net/ugc/37820376621127420/30BB01AF827A357D9D90A69C9894032C9CA994DF/?imw=1024&imh=320&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=true[/img]
[i]Executioner’s skill interrupts Dual Blader’s skill, causing a significant disadvantage in the ensuing fight.[/i]

This design allows champions to have distinct identities based on player skill. Some champions benefit from high mechanics, while others rely on decision-making. This variance affects lane matchups, strategy, and team compositions, creating more depth in draft strategies.

[h3]Tactics[/h3]

With the introduction of new game rules, we can now incorporate more strategic elements. Players will be able to adjust their overall game plan according to their preferred playstyle.

For example:
- If both the Top and Bottom lanes are picked for late-game scaling, they can be instructed to play defensively early on.
- If a team picks an early-game focused Jungler, tactics can be set so that the Jungler prioritizes ganks over farming, helping the weak lanes survive the early game.
[img]https://steamuserimages-a.akamaihd.net/ugc/37820376621153338/F2AD34AEF77BB34E41022E1FC9BB49A594269AAA/?imw=1024&imh=460&ima=fit&impolicy=Letterbox&imcolor=%23000000&letterbox=true[/img]
[i]A successful early-game engage setup that utilizes a ninja with a powerful initiation and a knight whose taunts generate an excellent response.[/i]

The goal is to make tactics an integral part of draft strategy while keeping the options intuitive and easy to use.

[h3]Technical Aspects[/h3]

So far, we've discussed the design direction of Teamfight Manager 2's match engine from a gameplay perspective. Now, let's dive into the technical challenges of implementing the match engine and how we're overcoming them. This section contains some technical details, so feel free to skip it if that's not your cup of tea!

[h3]Performance Issues[/h3]

In Teamfight Manager, the game rules were simple and each match lasted only one minute, which made the simulation relatively straightforward. Even so, that simplicity still imposed a significant load—primarily due to data collection. The Teamfight Manager series features dynamic in-game rules. As patches are applied, champion performance continuously shifts, and our ban/pick AI needs to respond accordingly.

To address this, our system continuously runs background simulations to collect data and adjust the AI based on the current patch. This process requires running an enormous number of simulations, so every match simulation must run as fast as possible.

Teamfight Manager 2, however, features a far more complex simulation. With the shift to MOBA-style rules, matches now last much longer than one minute, include more in-game objects, and introduce obstacles like walls that necessitate pathfinding, as well as asymmetric vision elements like bushes. On top of that, the AI controlling players is considerably more complex than before, which increases the overall computational load by several orders of magnitude.

To meet these challenges and achieve maximum optimization, Teamfight Manager 2 is being developed on a custom engine built in Rust.

[h3]Deterministic Simulation[/h3]

Saving every frame of a match would result in massive save file sizes. To avoid this, we ensure that if a match's initial state (seed, team strategies, champion selections, etc.) is identical, the simulation always yields the same outcome. This property, known as determinism, means that we only need to store the initial state to reliably replay any match—an enormous saving in storage space.

Moreover, for multiplayer, we only need to transmit the initial state to each client; each player can then run the simulation locally without sending the entire process over the network.

Achieving deterministic simulation requires careful handling of two key aspects:

- Randomness: Each match simulation uses its own random number generator initialized with a match-specific seed. While this isn’t overly challenging, care must be taken since third-party libraries can sometimes introduce unintended non-deterministic behavior.
- Floating-point Operations: Although floating-point math can be deterministic on the same PC, differences in hardware or environment can lead to discrepancies. Such discrepancies could cause players to see different outcomes in multiplayer, so we must eliminate these issues. Given that floating-point operations are also slower and the simulation doesn’t demand ultra-precise calculations, we’ve implemented all logic using integer-based fixed-point arithmetic.

[h3]Preprocessing Optimization[/h3]

Pathfinding and vision calculations are inherently slow. To minimize the computational cost, we divide the entire map into 32×32 pixel cells and precompute data for each cell.

For example, in pathfinding, we precompute and store the “next cell” needed to move from cell (a, b) to cell (c, d), allowing instantaneous pathfinding during simulation. Similarly, for vision, we precompute whether a cell at (a, b) can see a cell at (c, d), so the simulation can retrieve this information without any extra computation. While storing this data consumes a few megabytes of memory, it’s negligible on modern systems. Admittedly, this approach sacrifices a bit of precision—since calculations are based on 32-pixel segments—but the difference isn’t noticeable during gameplay.

[h3]Memory Allocation Optimization[/h3]

Our simulation demands frequent memory allocations and deallocations. Throughout a match, hundreds of projectiles are created and destroyed, and numerous buffs, champion deaths, and object respawns trigger continuous memory operations, which are computationally expensive.

Using a low-level language like Rust allows us to fine-tune memory management. We optimize the simulation by using a custom memory allocator that fits the unique needs of our game’s simulation structure.

[h3]Rendering Separation[/h3]

If a match isn’t being observed by a player, much of the rendering data is unnecessary. When running background simulations to gather results and statistics, we can skip generating rendering-related information. By distinguishing between these scenarios, we can significantly speed up background simulations by omitting the creation of rendering data.

[h3]Parallel Processing[/h3]

There’s a limit to the performance achievable on a single CPU core, so it’s crucial to utilize all available cores by running simulations in parallel. From the early stages of development, we designed the system to support smooth parallel processing.

Thanks to this approach, our current simulation can compute one minute of game time in about 0.05 to 0.1 seconds. While the exact time depends on PC performance and the number of parallel threads, on our current development machine, simulating 1,000 matches on 4 threads takes roughly 4 minutes (about 0.24 seconds per match). We continue to address technical challenges and optimize the match engine’s performance, staying true to our design vision while ensuring rapid execution.


Thank you for reading this lengthy post! We’ll see you again in the next development log!
